title: Ibn Khaldun
hook: the historian of Tunis who studied how societies rise and fall

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Battuta, who set out from Tangier for Mecca and kept going. Your line was: the traveler. Where did you go that was new to you? Day nine hundred fifty-one.

Damascus is under siege. Outside the walls is the army of Timur, the conqueror. Inside, a scholar from North Africa decides he wants to meet the man himself. The gates are closed, so his friends lower him down the city wall on ropes. He walks into the conqueror's camp and is received, and the two of them talk, about history, about kings, about the lands of the west. The scholar tells this story himself, in the account of his own life. His name was Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis, and he had spent years thinking about exactly this: why some peoples rise and conquer, and why their cities, in time, fall. Today: Ibn Khaldun.
screen: `DAMASCUS UNDER SIEGE.` → `LOWERED DOWN THE WALL ON ROPES.` → `A SCHOLAR MEETS A CONQUEROR.`

segments.voice: Ibn Khaldun served sultans across North Africa and al-Andalus, fell in and out of favor, spent time in prison, and finally withdrew to a quiet fortress to write. What he wrote first was an introduction to a history of the world, and the introduction took on a life of its own: the Muqaddimah, the introduction. His big idea has an Arabic name, asabiyya. Group feeling. The bond that holds a people together, the loyalty that makes them stand by each other. He saw it strongest among people who lived hard lives in the desert and the mountains, where nobody survives alone. That bond, he argued, is what lets a group win power and build a state. Then comes the city. Comfort. Fine clothes, soft beds, servants. Each generation inherits the power without the hardship that made it, and the bond quietly loosens. Rulers lean on paid soldiers instead of loyal kin. And one day a new group, with strong bonds and nothing to lose, comes in from the edge. Bonds build, luxury loosens. He was writing about dynasties, but the question travels: anyone can ask it of a family, a team or a mosque community. The Qur'an has a line some readers set beside his idea. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts." Ibn Khaldun wrote as a believing Muslim and a judge. For him, studying how societies rise and fall was a way of reading the world with open eyes.
screen: `A JUDGE WITHDRAWS TO WRITE.` · `ASABIYYA — GROUP FEELING.` · `HARDSHIP BINDS, COMFORT LOOSENS.` · `A NEW GROUP COMES IN FROM THE EDGE.` · then, large: `BONDS BUILD, LUXURY LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about your community's bonds. Settle, and breathe. Pick one group you belong to: a family, a group of friends, a congregation, a team at work. Ask Ibn Khaldun's question gently. What holds this group together? Was it stronger when things were harder? Where has comfort, or busyness, let the bond loosen a little? Don't blame anyone. Just notice. Then think of one person in that group you've drifted from. If you pray, you can hold that group before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Khaldun. The scholar born in Tunis whose Muqaddimah asks how group feeling builds a state, and how comfort loosens it. Today's word.
Your line: bonds build, luxury loosens. Today, do one small thing that strengthens a bond: call, visit, help, or simply show up. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah is read today by historians, sociologists and students of Islamic thought, and its idea of asabiyya, group feeling, is still discussed.
